clue.text: Reserve a garment, first securing leading designer listed here?

indicators.note: first tells us the garment phrase comes before the word for reserve, not after it
securing means holding something inside, so the garment phrase closes round the designer's letter

parts.note: a dress is a garment

indicators.note: the leading part of the word designer is its opening letter

parts.note: to book a table or seat is to reserve it

explanation.surface: A shopper reserves a dress that features a top designer's label, wondering where the details get written down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' reorders the charade: the clue gives the reserve word before the garment, but the garment phrase leads in the answer. 'leading designer' gives D.
explanation.definitionFit: Names, streets and phone numbers of contacts are recorded in this kind of personal directory, hence the cryptic 'listed here'.

clue.text: Peeled fruit cleric passed over to another priest

indicators.note: passed over is read as stretched across or covering, so the cleric's letters sit around the peeled fruit

parts.note: DD, Doctor of Divinity, is a clergyman's degree, standing for a cleric

indicators.note: peeling strips the skin, so the word fruit loses its outer letters

explanation.surface: A churchman handed some skinned fruit over to a fellow clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: DD (Doctor of Divinity) stands for a cleric. 'passed over' looks like being ignored for promotion, but here it signals one piece wrapping the other; 'Peeled' strips the outer letters of the printed word fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Druids were the priestly class of the ancient Celts, a different kind of priest from the cleric in the wordplay.

clue.text: Competitive dash calls for speed in reversing car

indicators.note: in places the turned-round car inside the word for speed

parts.note: rate is speed, as in the rate of travel

indicators.note: reversing a vehicle backs it up, so the word car is read backwards

explanation.surface: A frantic race needs plenty of pace even while backing the car out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversing' sits with car, so only that word turns; 'calls for' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes the frenzied competitive struggle of modern working life, likened to a scramble.

clue.text: Shaky start to A-levels

indicators.note: shaky suggests unsteady and wobbling, so the letters of start are jumbled

explanation.surface: A nervous pupil makes a wobbly beginning to their A-level exams.
explanation.walkthrough: The hyphen in 'A-levels' hides the split: the A is a separate piece and 'levels' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Strata are layers of rock or tiers of society, each one a level.

clue.text: Reckon being eaten by fish is just a hallucination

indicators.note: being eaten by puts the reckoning word inside the fish, as in its mouth

parts.note: bream is a freshwater fish
to add up is to reckon or calculate

explanation.surface: Fear of being devoured by a fish is just a nightmarish fancy.
explanation.definitionFit: A nightmare can feel real, like a hallucination, though it happens only in sleep.

clue.text: A half of cows like chewing this?

definitions.text: A half of cows like chewing this?

indicators.note: chewing mashes things up, so these letters are worked into a new order
half of the four-letter word cows is its opening pair

explanation.surface: Cattle munching away on the cattle feed, as half the herd seems to enjoy.
explanation.walkthrough: A, CO (half of 'cows') and LIKE are rearranged; the whole clue also describes what cattle do with this feed.
explanation.definitionFit: Oilcake is compressed seed residue after oil extraction, fed to cattle, so cows chew it.

clue.text: Cricket's over — dentist's work, too?

explanation.surface: At close of play the umpire's job is done, and so is the dentist's.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the umpires remove the stumps (the wooden posts) when play ends for the day; a dentist may extract the stumps of broken teeth.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking away the wickets marks the end of a day's cricket; pulling out old tooth roots is a dental extraction.

clue.text: Most impressed when girl in love got married

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, written as the letter O
Vera is a girl's name
wed means got married

explanation.surface: A girl in love who has just wed is overwhelmed with feeling.
explanation.definitionFit: To be overawed is to be filled with awe, so impressed to the point of being daunted.

clue.text: Church people converting Britney Spears

indicators.note: converting turns something into another form, so the pop star's name is rearranged

explanation.surface: A missionary church sets about converting the pop singer Britney Spears.
explanation.walkthrough: Religious 'converting' pairs neatly with the church definition, disguising the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Presbyterians belong to a Protestant church governed by elders, as in the Church of Scotland.

clue.text: Bound to speak with assurance

indicators.note: to speak tells us the word is said aloud and spelt by its sound

parts.note: bound means tied up, as a chicken is trussed

explanation.surface: Someone is obliged to talk with confidence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bound' looks like 'obliged', but here it is the past tense of tie up.
explanation.definitionFit: Trust is confidence or reliance placed in someone, a form of assurance.

clue.text: Covered left and right by this forage crop growing wild

indicators.note: growing wild means running out of control, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: A field of fodder spreading untamed covers ground on both sides.
explanation.definitionFit: Red clover is a pinkish-flowered legume sown as cattle fodder and to enrich soil.

clue.text: Had involvement in incident, attending a literary tea party

indicators.note: in puts the jumbled letters inside the word for incident

parts.note: a matter is an affair or incident, as in 'a police matter'

indicators.note: involvement suggests things involved, that is twisted and tangled, so the letters of had are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone was involved in an incident while at a book-world tea gathering.
explanation.walkthrough: 'involvement' reads as taking part, but signals that the letters of 'Had' are jumbled. The definition is loose: the character is identified by the famous tea party he attends.
explanation.definitionFit: The character from Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland hosts the famous tea party with the March Hare.

clue.text: The sort of cares that may burden landed folk

indicators.note: sort of hints at sorting letters into another order, so cares is rearranged

explanation.surface: The kind of worries that weigh down the landed gentry.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose: big estates of land are what landowners hold, and the clue jokes that they bring cares with them.
explanation.definitionFit: Landowners' estates are measured in units of area, so plenty of them is what landed folk carry.

clue.text: Plant in the stable?

explanation.surface: Someone asks what greenery is growing in the stable.
explanation.walkthrough: Sorrel is a sour-leaved herb; it is also a chestnut colour of horse, which lives in a stable.
explanation.definitionFit: Sorrel is a leafy herb, and a reddish-brown horse is also called by this name.

clue.text: Going round rock, climbing into a crack

indicators.note: in a down clue, climbing means the word is read from bottom to top, so it runs backwards

parts.note: a tor is a rocky hilltop or outcrop

indicators.note: to crack something is to break it apart, so the letters of the word into are reassembled

explanation.surface: A climber goes round a boulder and wedges into a fissure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crack' looks like a climber's fissure but is the anagram signal, turning 'into' into TION; 'climbing' in a down clue sends the rock word upwards, giving ROT.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotation is the act of turning on an axis, which is moving round.

clue.text: Die out, as did the Cheshire Cat?

explanation.surface: Something vanishes, just like a famous grinning cat.
explanation.walkthrough: In Alice's Adventures in Wonderland the Cheshire Cat slowly vanishes until only its grin remains.
explanation.definitionFit: To die out is to dwindle and disappear, which is how the grinning cat vanished bit by bit.

clue.text: Purpose of a duvet cover being pinned to the floor

explanation.surface: A wrestler's opponent is pinned down like a quilt in its cover.
explanation.walkthrough: A duvet cover contains the duvet's filling of feathers, so it keeps the down in place: the first reading is a pun.
explanation.definitionFit: A cover keeps soft feathers contained, a joke sense; separately, pinning someone to the ground means restraining them.

clue.text: Ten I'd let out, as permitted

indicators.note: out means put out of order, so the letters of the preceding words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone let ten people out, as was allowed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let out' looks like a phrase, but 'let' is part of the fodder and only 'out' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To be entitled to something is to have the right to it, so allowed it.

clue.text: Cry, when the hunt's off

parts.note: the call huntsmen give on sighting a fox, which sets the hunt off and running

explanation.surface: A shout goes up when the hunt is cancelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like called off, but here it means started, as in 'they're off'.
explanation.definitionFit: The traditional shout of a huntsman when the quarry is sighted and the chase begins.

clue.text: Bristle when newlywed embraces first love

indicators.note: embraces means holds within arms, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: a bride is a woman who has just married

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the word love

explanation.surface: A just-married woman hugs her first sweetheart and her new husband bristles.
explanation.definitionFit: To bridle is to show anger or resentment, as a horse throws back its head; bristle means the same.

clue.text: Views with respect

explanation.surface: Someone looks on with esteem.
explanation.walkthrough: As a verb it means looks at or considers; as a noun it is the respectful good wishes ending a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: To regard is to look at or consider; good wishes sent respectfully are also given by this word.

clue.text: Islam's reformulated religious book

indicators.note: reformulated means made up again in a new form, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the apostrophe is ignored and the S counts as a letter of the fodder

explanation.surface: A rewritten version of Islam's teaching appears in a holy text.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive S is needed here: all six letters of ISLAMS are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A missal is the Roman Catholic book containing the texts for celebrating Mass.

clue.text: This digit's worth three bits

parts.note: computing sense: a base-eight figure holds exactly the information of three binary digits

explanation.surface: Someone appraises a finger as worth very little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bits' looks like small coins or pieces; here it means binary digits, and eight values need three of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A base-eight number system uses digits 0 to 7, each represented by three binary digits.

clue.text: Wild beast I tagged initially, zoo intended setting free

indicators.note: setting free releases things from their order, so all these letters are rearranged
initially takes the opening letters of the two words that follow it

explanation.surface: A keeper tagged an animal the zoo meant to release into the wild.
explanation.walkthrough: I TAGGED plus Z and I, the first letters of 'zoo intended', are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The dziggetai is the kiang or onager of Mongolia, an untamed Asian ass.

clue.text: Wind making one initially tack to port, maybe?

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of the word tack

parts.note: port is one example of a wine, hence the maybe

explanation.surface: A breeze makes a yacht tack towards the harbour side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making one' joins the two pieces into one word. 'tack' and 'port' look like sailing terms; port is the fortified drink, and 'Wind' is the verb, as in coiling string.
explanation.definitionFit: Twine is string; as a verb it means to twist or coil, which is to wind.

clue.text: New poems you composed for Rebecca, for example — or Justine?

definitions.note: these are novels named after their heroines; the answer is the adjective describing such a title character

indicators.note: composed means put together, as a writer arranges words, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer produces fresh verses for a woman named Rebecca, or maybe one named Justine.
explanation.walkthrough: Rebecca (Daphne du Maurier) and Justine (Sade, also Durrell) are novels named for their heroines, so 'for' belongs to the surface link.
explanation.definitionFit: A title character who gives her name to the book is described by this adjective.

clue.text: Check key is inside — that's the rule

indicators.note: is inside places the key's letter within the word for check

parts.note: to rein in is to check or restrain
G is a musical key

explanation.surface: Someone makes sure the key is indoors, as house policy demands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Check' looks like verify, but it means restrain, as with a horse's reins.
explanation.definitionFit: A monarch's reign is the period of their rule.

clue.text: Applied at time when there's trouble afoot

definitions.text: Applied at time when there's trouble afoot

parts.words: Applied at time when there's trouble afoot
parts.note: afoot is taken literally: the trouble is on the foot, and this small pad is stuck on to ease it

explanation.surface: Something is brought in whenever trouble is brewing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble afoot' usually means mischief brewing; here it is a painful hard patch of skin on the toe.
explanation.definitionFit: A small medicated pad stuck over a hard patch of skin on the toe to relieve pressure.
